body:
Scientific discoveries and their importance

Science develops through observation, questions, explanations and evidence. A scientist may discover a previously unknown phenomenon, explain how a natural process works, develop a mathematical theory or establish an institution where scientific research can continue.

Indian scientists have made important contributions to physics, mathematics, biology, agriculture, atomic energy and space research. Their achievements are best understood by connecting each scientist with the correct field, contribution and year.

C. V. Raman and the scattering of light

Sir Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman (1888-1970) was an Indian physicist best known for discovering the Raman effect on 28 February 1928. He made this discovery while working at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta, now Kolkata.

When light passes through a transparent substance, some of it is scattered in different directions. Most of this scattered light retains the wavelength of the incoming light. However, a small fraction has a different wavelength because light exchanges energy with the molecules of the substance. This change in wavelength is called the Raman effect.

The discovery demonstrated that scattered light can provide information about the molecular properties of matter. It became an important foundation for Raman spectroscopy, which is used to identify and study substances.

Scattering is not always the Raman effect. In ordinary elastic scattering, light changes direction without changing wavelength. In Raman scattering, a small fraction of scattered light changes wavelength. The blue appearance of a clear sky is explained mainly by Rayleigh scattering, not the Raman effect.

Nobel Prize and National Science Day

Raman received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930 for his work on the scattering of light and the discovery of the effect named after him. He was also awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1954.

India observes National Science Day on 28 February to commemorate the discovery made on 28 February 1928. The first National Science Day was celebrated in 1987. The occasion promotes scientific awareness, curiosity and the application of science in society.

Prelims focus

  • C. V. Raman discovered the Raman effect on 28 February 1928.
  • The Raman effect concerns a change in the wavelength of scattered light.
  • Raman received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics.
  • He received the Bharat Ratna in 1954.
  • 28 February is National Science Day; its first celebration was in 1987.
  • Trap: The Raman effect and Rayleigh scattering are not the same phenomenon.

[Sources: NCERT, Curiosity: Science, Standard 6, Chapter 1, 'The Wonderful World of Science,' printed pp. 5-7; Nobel Prize, 'Sir Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman: Biographical,' section on the 1928 discovery and 1930 award; National Council of Science Museums, '28th February, National Science Day in India,' sections 'What is Raman Effect?' and 'When was the day declared?'; Press Information Bureau, 'National Science Day 2025,' 27 February 2025. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

body:
Why the 2 scientists must be distinguished

Two important Indian physicists share the surname Bose, but their principal achievements belong to different areas of science. Jagadish Chandra Bose worked on radio waves and responses in plants. Satyendra Nath Bose developed ideas in quantum physics that became the foundation of Bose-Einstein statistics.

Jagadish Chandra Bose: Radio waves and plant responses

Jagadish Chandra Bose (1858-1937) was a physicist and plant scientist. During the 1890s, he conducted pioneering experiments involving radio and microwave-frequency electromagnetic waves. This research contributed to the early scientific development of wireless communication.

Radio waves are a form of electromagnetic radiation. Like visible light, they can travel through a vacuum, although they have much longer wavelengths. Bose studied their properties through experimental investigation.

He also investigated how plants respond to changes in their surroundings. His studies showed that plants produce measurable responses to stimuli and that electrical changes can be associated with some plant activities. These findings contributed to the scientific study of plant physiology.

Bose's experiments demonstrated measurable responses in plants. They do not establish that plants possess an animal-like brain or nervous system. His contributions to radio-wave research should also not be confused with a claim that he alone invented all wireless communication.

He founded the Bose Institute in Calcutta on 30 November 1917. The institution supported research across physics, plant science and other scientific disciplines.

Satyendra Nath Bose: Quantum statistics

Satyendra Nath Bose (1894-1974) was a theoretical physicist. In 1924, he developed a new statistical treatment of light particles. Albert Einstein recognised the importance of this work and extended the underlying ideas to certain material particles.

The resulting framework is known as Bose-Einstein statistics. A class of particles called bosons is named in honour of Satyendra Nath Bose. At the school level, the important idea is that certain particles can occupy the same quantum state, whereas no 2 identical fermions can occupy the same quantum state.

Einstein's extension helped predict the possibility of a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). In this unusual state of matter, a dilute gas cooled to an extremely low temperature can exhibit collective quantum behaviour.

Who received the 2001 Nobel Prize?

Bose-Einstein condensation was experimentally achieved in dilute atomic gases in 1995. The 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to Eric A. Cornell, Wolfgang Ketterle and Carl E. Wieman for achieving Bose-Einstein condensation and studying its properties.

Satyendra Nath Bose did not receive the 2001 Nobel Prize. His name is associated with the theoretical foundation, whereas the 2001 prize recognised later experimental achievements.

Comparison of the 2 scientists

ScientistMain fieldsKey association
Jagadish Chandra BosePhysics and plant physiologyEarly radio-wave experiments; plant responses; Bose Institute, 1917
Satyendra Nath BoseTheoretical and quantum physicsBose-Einstein statistics, 1924; bosons; theoretical foundation of BEC

Prelims focus

  • Jagadish Chandra Bose: radio waves, plant responses and Bose Institute.
  • Bose Institute: founded in Kolkata on 30 November 1917.
  • Satyendra Nath Bose: Bose-Einstein statistics, 1924.
  • Bose-Einstein condensation was experimentally achieved in 1995.
  • The 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Cornell, Ketterle and Wieman.
  • Trap: Satyendra Nath Bose was not a recipient of the 2001 Nobel Prize.

[Sources: Department of Science and Technology, 'DST - Bose Institute,' institutional history and research fields; Department of Science and Technology, 'Dignitaries Trace the Evolution of Quantum Mechanics on 100 Years of S. N. Bose's Colossal Work,' section on the 1924 paper; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 1, 'Matter in Our Surroundings,' printed p. 10, 'Bose-Einstein Condensate'; Nobel Prize, 'The Nobel Prize in Physics 2001,' press release dated 9 October 2001. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Jagadish Chandra Bose and Satyendra Nath Bose: Two Different Scientific Contributions

body:
Mathematics as a foundation of science

Mathematics helps scientists describe patterns, compare quantities and develop explanations of natural phenomena. Indian mathematical contributions extend from early astronomy and arithmetic to modern number theory and statistics.

Srinivasa Ramanujan: Number theory

Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887-1920) was an Indian mathematician born on 22 December 1887 in Erode, in present-day Tamil Nadu. He became internationally recognised for important contributions to number theory, infinite series, continued fractions and mathematical analysis.

Number theory studies the properties and relationships of integers, such as divisibility and patterns among whole numbers. Ramanujan discovered numerous mathematical relationships and developed results that later mathematicians continued to investigate.

In 1913, Ramanujan began corresponding with the British mathematician G. H. Hardy at Cambridge. Hardy recognised the importance of Ramanujan's work, and the 2 mathematicians subsequently collaborated.

Ramanujan was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 1918. The abbreviation FRS refers to membership of a scientific society; it is not a Nobel Prize.

National Mathematics Day

India observes National Mathematics Day on 22 December, Ramanujan's birth anniversary. The Government of India announced the observance in 2011, and 2012 was celebrated as the National Mathematics Year.

28 February: National Science Day, associated with C. V. Raman. 22 December: National Mathematics Day, associated with Srinivasa Ramanujan.

Earlier Indian mathematicians and astronomers

Aryabhata was an Indian mathematician and astronomer. His work Aryabhatiya, composed around 499 CE, included important mathematical and astronomical ideas. He is associated with calculations involving planetary motions and the rotation of the Earth.

Brahmagupta was another important Indian mathematician and astronomer. His work Brahmasphutasiddhanta, written in 628 CE, gave systematic mathematical rules involving zero and negative numbers.

The history of zero developed over a long period. It is therefore inaccurate to attribute the entire development of zero to a single scientist without qualification.

Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis: Statistics

Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis (1893-1972) was an Indian statistician. Statistics involves collecting, organising and interpreting data so that meaningful conclusions can be drawn.

Mahalanobis founded the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Calcutta in 1931. His work helped establish statistics as an important field of scientific research and its application to large-scale surveys and national planning. He is also associated with the statistical measure called Mahalanobis distance, used to compare observations while taking several characteristics into account.

Important distinctions

NameFieldPrincipal association
AryabhataMathematics and astronomyAryabhatiya, about 499 CE
BrahmaguptaMathematics and astronomyRules involving zero and negative numbers, 628 CE
Srinivasa RamanujanPure mathematicsNumber theory; FRS, 1918
P. C. MahalanobisStatisticsIndian Statistical Institute, 1931

Prelims focus

  • Srinivasa Ramanujan: number theory and mathematical analysis.
  • 1913: Ramanujan began corresponding with G. H. Hardy.
  • 1918: Ramanujan became a Fellow of the Royal Society.
  • 22 December: National Mathematics Day.
  • P. C. Mahalanobis: statistics and establishment of ISI in 1931.
  • Trap: Aryabhata the mathematician and Aryabhata the satellite are not the same subject.

[Sources: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, Chapter 5, 'India's Heritage of Science and Technology,' printed pp. 37-42; Royal Society, certificate of election of Srinivasa Ramanujan, record EC/1918/18, dated 2 May 1918; Press Information Bureau, 'National Mathematics Day: Tribute to Legendary Indian Mathematician,' 22 December 2022; Indian Statistical Institute, 'Brief History of the Institute,' section on its establishment in 1931. body:
What does astrophysics study?

Astrophysics applies the principles of physics to objects in space, including the Sun, other stars and galaxies. Scientists study the light emitted by stars to understand their temperatures, composition and physical conditions. They also use physical theories to explain how stars form, change and eventually reach the final stages of their lives.

Two Indian-born scientists associated with major developments in this field are Meghnad Saha and Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Their achievements address different questions.

Meghnad Saha: Thermal ionisation of gases

Meghnad Saha (1893-1956) was an Indian physicist and astrophysicist. In 1920, he developed an important theory of thermal ionisation, commonly associated with the Saha ionisation equation.

Ionisation occurs when an atom or molecule gains or loses electrons and becomes electrically charged. In sufficiently hot gases, atoms can lose electrons. Saha established a relationship connecting the degree of ionisation with conditions such as temperature and pressure.

This helped scientists interpret the spectra of stars. A spectrum is the pattern of different wavelengths of light received from a source. The spectral lines observed from a star depend not only on the elements present but also on physical conditions in its atmosphere.

Meghnad Saha, 1920: thermal ionisation theory, used in understanding the physical conditions of stellar atmospheres.

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar: Stellar structure and evolution

Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar (1910-1995) was an Indian-born astrophysicist. His theoretical studies helped explain the structure and evolution of stars, including how physical forces and internal conditions affect a star over time.

He is particularly associated with the theory of white dwarfs, which are dense stellar remnants. A well-known result of his work is the Chandrasekhar limit, which concerns the maximum mass at which a white dwarf can remain supported by electron-degeneracy pressure. The detailed mathematics of this result is beyond the present level; the important association is with stellar structure and evolution.

Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics, sharing the prize with William A. Fowler. Chandrasekhar was recognised for theoretical studies of physical processes important to the structure and evolution of stars.

How their contributions differ

Saha's work primarily helps explain what the light from a star reveals about its atmosphere. Chandrasekhar's work helps explain the physical structure of stars and how they evolve. Both belong to astrophysics, but they are not the same discovery.

ScientistPrincipal workYear or recognition
Meghnad SahaThermal ionisation theory and stellar spectra1920
Subrahmanyan ChandrasekharTheoretical studies of stellar structure and evolutionNobel Prize in Physics, 1983

Prelims focus

  • Meghnad Saha: thermal ionisation theory, 1920.
  • Saha's work helped explain the spectra of stars.
  • Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar: stellar structure and evolution.
  • Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
  • Trap: The Saha ionisation equation and the Chandrasekhar limit describe different aspects of astrophysics.

[Sources: Indian National Science Academy, Biographical Memoirs: Meghnad Saha, section on the 1920 theory of high-temperature ionisation; Indian National Science Academy, Megh Nad Saha, introductory discussion of the theory's application to stellar spectra; Nobel Prize, 'The 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics,' press release dated 19 October 1983. Online sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
